# Blue-green upgrades
 
You can perform blue-green upgrades to reduce downtime, but only for incremental patch releases in a release series that is certified as blue-green compatible. We certify a release series as blue-green compatible when we have successfully tested the following:

1. The current and target incremental patch releases in that series can run together during the upgrade
1. You can roll back the deployment without major issues

@include 'beta.mdx'

## Blue-green planning checklist

The following checklist is an overview of the steps for conducting a rolling, blue-green upgrade with minimal downtime:

- [ ] Verify that Terraform Enterprise is deployed to a non-Nomad runtime. Refer to [Prerequisites](#prerequisites).
- [ ] Select a target version and confirm its compatibility with your environments and with blue-green upgrades. Blue-green deployments are only available for select incremental patch releases. Refer to [Releases](/terraform/enterprise/releases/2.1.x) for more information.
- [ ] Take a live backup of PostgreSQL and blob storage. You do not need to back up Redis.
- [ ] Download the container images for the target release.
- [ ] Run the [pre-upgrade checks](/terraform/enterprise/deploy/manage/upgrade/pre-checks) for your runtime and resolve any failures or warnings.
- [ ] Define rollback criteria and rehearse the rollback procedure.
- [ ] Upgrade Terraform Enterprise.

## Prerequisites

Before you plan a blue-green upgrade, ensure you meet all prerequisites:

1. Terraform Enterprise is running in an active-active configuration with at least two instances.
1. Terraform Enterprise is not running on Nomad.
1. Terraform Enterprise is running an incremental patch release in a release series that is certified as blue-green compatible.
1. You are an advanced Terraform Enterprise operator who is confident with the primitives of your autoscaling group, load balancer, and deployment runtime.
1. For Kubernetes and OpenShift, you must enable graceful draining as a pre-stop lifecycle method, which requires version 2.1.2 or later of the Helm chart. Enabling graceful draining requires a one-time downtime for a Terraform Enterprise deployment. Refer to [Enable graceful draining](#enable-graceful-draining) for instructions.

## Enable graceful draining

This requires version 2.1.2 or later of the Helm chart.
For Kubernetes or OpenShift deployments, add the following configuration to your `values.yaml` file:

  ```yaml
  waitForDrain:
    enabled: true
  ```

Next, take the full cluster offline so that you can conduct a Helm upgrade. Changes to lifecycle hooks do not apply to existing pods, and the existing pods do not wait gracefully for draining. When a pod stops, it automatically triggers a node drain and then waits for tasks to finish. Draining can take up to 24 hours but is often faster. 

You do not need to conduct the upgrade at the same time. As long as the `waitForDrain` configuration is in your `values.yaml` file, taking the cluster offline is a one-time instance of downtime.

If you do not enable graceful draining, the rolling upgrade terminates pods without waiting for tasks to finish, which can lead to unexpected errors.

You can confirm that pre-stop is enabled on a Kubernetes pod:

```shell-session
$ kubectl get pod <POD_NAME> -n <NAMESPACE> -o yaml
```

Under `spec.containers`, find the Terraform Enterprise container and confirm that its `lifecycle.preStop` hook contains the configured pre-stop command. Also confirm that `spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds` is set to `86400`, which is 24 hours.


## Select a target version

Identify the Terraform Enterprise version you plan to install. Check the release notes for the target version to confirm that it supports a blue-green upgrade from your current version. Compare the supported platforms and dependency versions in the [release tables](/terraform/enterprise/releases) with your current infrastructure. Review the release notes for the target version and every intermediate version for breaking changes, deprecations, and new requirements.

Download the Terraform Enterprise container images for every release in your upgrade path. Import the images into internal registries or hosts that cannot reach the public registry so you can update configuration files without extending downtime. Prune unused local images or volumes to free capacity where needed.

@include 'software-compatibility-report.mdx'

## Take a live backup of PostgreSQL and blob storage

We test blue-green compatible releases to ensure that upgrades do not mutate the state of Redis or the database, but you should still follow best practices for recovering data if something unexpected happens. Take a live backup of your PostgreSQL database and blob storage so that you can restore them after rolling back. A live backup is a backup of a datastore taken while the application is still running. You do not need to back up Redis because it stores the job queue and not critical data. Use native tools, such as `pg_dump` for PostgreSQL and AWS Backup for blob storage, to conduct these backups. Refer to [Back up and restore Terraform Enterprise](/terraform/enterprise/deploy/manage/backup-restore) for general backup guidance.

## Conduct the blue-green upgrade

After you capture backups, apply the target release. Use the artifacts you staged during planning so you can complete these steps within the maintenance window.

1. Update your configuration to reference the staged Terraform Enterprise image for the target [release](/terraform/enterprise/releases): `images.releases.hashicorp.com/hashicorp/terraform-enterprise:<TARGET_VERSION>`.

<Tabs>
<Tab heading="Docker and Podman" group="first">

Podman Kube and Docker Compose do not explicitly support zero-downtime upgrades. However, if you used a HashiCorp Validated Design to deploy Terraform Enterprise on virtual machines in AWS, GCP, or Azure, you can perform a zero-downtime upgrade with the following steps.

First, update the deployment configuration to use the target image tag without starting an automatic rollout:

- For an AWS Auto Scaling group (ASG), update the launch template version used by the group. Do not start an instance refresh before draining the instances.
- For a GCP Managed Instance Group (MIG), update the instance template used by the group and select an opportunistic update policy. Refer to Google's documentation about [opportunistic updates](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instance-groups/updating-migs#set_up_a_proactive_or_an_opportunistic_update).
- For an Azure Virtual Machine Scale Set (VMSS), set the upgrade policy to manual before updating the scale set model. Refer to Azure's documentation about [manual upgrade policy mode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/virtual-machine-scale-sets-upgrade-policy#manual-upgrade-policy-mode).

Then follow these steps for one instance at a time. Keep the other instances running and confirm they have enough capacity to handle the workload:

1. Connect to the Terraform Enterprise container on the instance you plan to replace and drain that node:

    ```shell-session
    $ tfectl node drain
    ```

    Wait for the node to be ready to be terminated. You can check the status using the `tfectl node tasks` command on the instance. Do not add the `--all` flag, which drains every node. Draining every node causes downtime. Refer to [Gracefully stop work on a node](/terraform/enterprise/deploy/reference/cli#gracefully-stop-work-on-a-node) for more information.

1. Remove the drained instance from the load balancer and wait for any in-flight requests to finish.

1. Replace or update only the drained instance using the target configuration:
   - For AWS, terminate the instance without decreasing the group's desired capacity so the ASG creates a replacement.
   - For GCP, use the MIG's recreate operation for the instance rather than deleting it from the group.
   - For Azure, manually apply the updated scale set model to the selected instance. Reimage it if the configuration change requires it. Do not assume deleting an instance automatically creates a replacement.

1. Confirm that the updated or replacement instance runs the target Terraform Enterprise version and passes the startup and readiness checks in [Validate the blue-green upgrade](#validate-the-blue-green-upgrade).

1. Return the healthy instance to the load balancer. If registration is automatic, ensure the load balancer sends traffic only after the instance passes its health checks.

1. Confirm that the instance serves traffic successfully before moving to the next one. If validation fails, stop the rollout and follow your rollback criteria.

After you replace every instance, confirm that the upgrade is complete:

1. Connect to the Terraform Enterprise container on any instance and list all active nodes:

    ```shell-session
    $ tfectl node list
    ```

1. Confirm that the list contains the number of nodes you expect and no node from a previous instance.
1. Connect to the Terraform Enterprise container on each node in the list and verify that it runs the target version:

    ```shell-session
    $ tfectl app version
    ```

The upgrade is complete when every node in the list reports the target version.

If you are not running Terraform Enterprise behind an autoscaling group, follow the same drain, remove, replace, and validate sequence, but create the replacement instance manually. The specifics vary based on your deployment configuration.

</Tab>
<Tab heading="Helm chart" group="second">

Update your existing `values.yaml` file with the new image tag and rollout strategy. Keep the top-level `replicaCount` at your current value of at least two, and keep `waitForDrain.enabled` set to `true`:

```yaml
image:
  repository: images.releases.hashicorp.com
  name: hashicorp/terraform-enterprise
  tag: <TARGET_VERSION>
```

Then conduct a Helm rolling upgrade. Replace the placeholders with your values:

```shell-session
$ helm -n <TFE_NAMESPACE> upgrade \
    terraform-enterprise hashicorp/terraform-enterprise \
    --version=<HELM_CHART_VERSION> \
    --values=<OVERRIDES_FILE> \
    --wait \
    --timeout <HOURS>h
```

Optionally, set `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` under `strategy.rollingUpdate` in your values file or as Helm command-line flags. These values control the rollout behavior. The default field for `strategy.type` is `RollingUpdate`. Do not change the default for `strategy.type`.

In the worst case, the upgrade takes 24 hours multiplied by the number of pods, for example two days for two pods. Your `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable` values can change this estimate. Monitor tasks on each drained pod with the `tfectl node tasks` command, and manually stop unresponsive tasks to speed up the upgrade. Set the `--timeout` value in the Helm command to match your estimate.

</Tab>
<Tab heading="Nomad" group="fourth">

Terraform Enterprise running on Nomad does not support blue-green upgrades with a graceful shutdown.

</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Validate the blue-green upgrade

Perform these checks during the upgrade, after it, or both.

1. **Verify startup checks passed**. Use the Terraform Enterprise CLI to trigger and review startup checks. Refer to [Trigger startup checks](/terraform/enterprise/deploy/reference/cli#trigger-startup-checks) for instructions on running the checks and [Startup checks reference](/terraform/enterprise/deploy/reference/startup-checks) for details about each check and common failure scenarios.

1. **Check application health**. Query the [readiness endpoint](/terraform/enterprise/api-docs/readiness) to verify the application responds correctly. The endpoint returns `200 OK` when the node is ready to accept requests. The readiness endpoint reports the status of a single node, so in multi-node deployments query each node directly rather than through a load balancer, which may route the request to any node. Refer to [Perform diagnostics](/terraform/enterprise/deploy/troubleshoot/perform-diagnostics#check-node-readiness) for additional information about checking node readiness.

   ```shell-session
   $ curl https://<TFE_HOSTNAME>/api/v1/health/readiness
   ```

1. **Perform a test run**. Execute a test Terraform plan and apply in a non-production workspace to confirm core functionality.

1. **Verify release-specific features**. Confirm that features or fixes from the target release appear as expected. Consult the release notes for validation steps.

1. **Document the upgrade**. Record the upgrade path, any issues encountered, and resolution steps for future reference.

## Troubleshoot blue-green upgrades

If a validation step fails or the application does not stabilize:

1. Pause the rollout so no additional instances or pods are replaced.
1. Review application logs for migration errors or dependency mismatches. Refer to [Access the Terraform Enterprise CLI](/terraform/enterprise/deploy/manage/access-cli) for instructions on accessing logs in your environment. You can also download logs through the [Admin Console](/terraform/enterprise/deploy/manage/access-admin-console) or the [System API](/terraform/enterprise/api-docs/support-bundle).
1. Roll back with zero downtime by repeating the upgrade steps one instance or pod at a time with the previous image tag.
1. Contact [HashiCorp Support](https://www.ibm.com/mysupport) with collected logs, the upgrade path attempted, and error messages for assistance.
